summary: Describes the Handover Keying (HOKEY) problem of re-authenticating quickly when a mobile device moves between access points. The existing EAP key framework forces a full EAP exchange again, which causes long delays. It states design goals for reusing derived keying material in handovers. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5169 explains why a phone that moves between access points takes too long to get back on the network. It describes the design goals for a handover keying protocol that reuses the keys from the first login, and the security rules such a protocol must follow.

subtitle: The case for reusing session keys when a phone moves, instead of starting over.

tldr.problem: Every time a mobile device moves to a new access point, the EAP framework makes it run a full authentication exchange with its home server, and the round trips that costs make the handover too slow.
tldr.mechanism: The document describes the problem and sets out design goals for a handover keying protocol, or HOKEY, that reuses the keying material from the first authentication and can run the re-authentication against a nearby server.
tldr.outcome: Nothing is implemented here. The document scopes the work to handovers within one administrative domain and leaves inter-domain handover outside its scope.

facts.label: Round trips to reach the EAP server

today: RFC 5169 is an Informational document and is not listed as obsoleted or updated. It is the problem statement and the design goals for HOKEY, the IETF handover keying work, and it describes a protocol that had not yet been written.

sections.title: Introduction: Why Handover Is Slow
sections.content:
The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP), specified in RFC 3748, is a generic framework supporting multiple authentication methods. Its primary purpose is network access control, and it also supports exporting session keys derived during the authentication. The EAP keying hierarchy defines two keys derived at the top level, the Master Session Key (MSK) and the Extended Master Session Key (EMSK).

In most deployments, an EAP peer and an EAP server authenticate each other through a third party, the pass-through authenticator, which encapsulates EAP packets from the network access technology within the Authentication, Authorization and Accounting (AAA) protocol. The authenticator does not take part in the EAP exchange itself and simply acts as a gateway while the EAP method runs. After a successful authentication, the EAP server transports the MSK to the authenticator using AAA protocols, and the underlying layer 2 or layer 3 protocol derives further keys from the MSK, including the transient session keys used for per-packet encryption and authentication. While the authenticator is one logical device, several physical devices may be involved: the CAPWAP model of RFC 3990 splits it into Wireless Termination Points and Access Controllers.

Wireless handover between access points or base stations is a complex process involving several layers of protocol execution, and it often produces delays that are unacceptable for real-time applications such as voice. One part of that process is EAP re-authentication, which can contribute significantly to the overall handover time, so lowering re-authentication time lowers the handover time.

When a peer arrives at a new authenticator, existing implementations run an EAP method regardless of whether the peer was recently authenticated and still holds unexpired keying material. The exchange starts with an EAP-Response/Identity message from the peer, continues with one or more round trips between the EAP server and the peer, and ends with EAP-Success or EAP-Failure. At a minimum the exchange is 1.5 round trips, but given how EAP interacts with AAA and that an identity exchange is typically used, at least 2 round trips are required to reach the EAP server. The most commonly used EAP methods need more: EAP-TLS requires at least 3, and typically 4 or more, round trips.
sections.plainLanguage: EAP is the framework a device uses to prove who it is before it gets on the network. When the device moves to a new access point, the current setup throws that proof away and starts again from scratch, with several exchanges of messages over a link that may reach the other side of the world.

sections.title: Problem Statement
sections.content:
Under the existing model, any re-authentication requires a full EAP exchange with the EAP server the peer originally authenticated to. That introduces handover latency from both network transit time and processing delay. In a service provider network the peer's home EAP server may be on the other side of the world, and typical intercontinental latencies across the Internet are 100 to 300 milliseconds per round trip. Processing delays average a couple of milliseconds for symmetric-key operations and hundreds of milliseconds for public-key operations.

An EAP conversation with a full method run takes two or more round trips to complete, which delays re-authentication and handover. Some methods can use keys and state from the initial authentication to finish a later authentication in fewer round trips and without public-key operations, but even there multiple round trips to the EAP server are required, which gives unacceptable handover times.

The document draws out the conclusions. It is undesirable to run an EAP Identity and a complete EAP method exchange each time a peer authenticates to a new authenticator or extends its current authentication with the same authenticator. A method-independent, efficient re-authentication protocol is desirable. Keying material from the initial authentication can be used to enable efficient re-authentication. It is also desirable to have a local server with low-latency connectivity to the peer that can facilitate re-authentication. Finally, a re-authentication protocol should support cases where an EAP server passes authentication information to a remote re-authentication server, so that a peer can re-authenticate locally without contacting its home re-authentication server.
sections.plainLanguage: The delay has two sources: the time a message spends crossing the network, and the time each side spends computing an answer. Both are significant when the server is far away. The document's answer is to reuse the keys from the first login and to put a server close to the device that can handle the re-login itself.

sections.title: Design Goals
sections.content:
The protocol MUST be responsive to the handover and re-authentication latency objectives of a mobile access network, and a solution that reduces latency compared with a full EAP authentication is the most favourable, because in networks that rely on reactive re-authentication this directly affects handover times. Any keying hierarchy and protocol defined MUST be lower-layer independent, so that it can work over heterogeneous technologies, although it MAY require some additional support from the lower layers without requiring any particular one.

Changes to existing EAP methods MUST NOT be required, and there MUST be no requirements imposed on future EAP methods, provided they satisfy the EAP keying and RFC 4017 specifications. Only the EAP methods that currently conform to those specifications need independence, and in particular methods that do not generate the required keys need not be supported.

Any modifications to EAP and EAP keying MUST be compatible with RADIUS and Diameter, extensions to both being acceptable, and the designs must be configurable to satisfy the AAA key management requirements of RFC 4962. Compatibility and coexistence with compliant EAP deployments MUST be provided: a peer that does not support fast re-authentication should still work in a network that supports it, and a peer that does support it should still work in a network that does not.

Any re-authentication protocol MUST support cryptographic algorithm agility, to avoid hard-coded primitives whose security may later prove to be compromised, and MAY support algorithm negotiation provided it does not adversely affect overall performance, for instance by requiring additional round trips. Finally, the protocol MAY make changes to the peer, the authenticator and the EAP server as needed to meet the goals, and should seek to minimise those changes without sacrificing performance, to make deployment easier.
sections.plainLanguage: The goals are deliberately narrow. The mechanism must not depend on the wireless technology underneath, must not require changes to any existing authentication method, must work over the accounting and authorization systems operators already run, and must still work when one side of the connection is too old to support it.

sections.title: Security Goals
sections.content:
The security goals are drawn from the guidance in RFC 4962. Any key must have a well-defined scope, must be used in a specific context and for the intended use, and the lifetime and scope of each key must be defined clearly so that every entity allowed to hold the key has the same context during the validity period. In a hierarchical key structure, the lifetime of lower-level keys must not exceed the lifetime of higher-level keys, which may imply that context and scope parameters have to be exchanged, with defined semantics so that channel binding can be specified.

If a key hierarchy is deployed, compromising lower-level keys must not compromise the higher-level keys they were derived from, and the compromise of keys at one level must not compromise other keys at the same level. The same applies to the entities holding those keys: compromising keys on one authenticator must not reveal the keys of another. The compromise of higher-level keys does carry security implications for the lower levels. All keying material must be uniquely named so it can be managed effectively, and guidance on caching, storage and deletion must be defined in a solution document.

A fresh key is one generated for its intended use, so the hierarchy must provide for creating multiple cryptographically separate child keys from a root key, and for refreshing each key in the hierarchy. Each handover keying participant must be authenticated to the parties it communicates with to the extent needed to ensure proper key scoping, and must securely provide its identity to any entity that needs it to define the key scope.

On authorization, the EAP key management document discusses vulnerabilities common to handover mechanisms, including the way authorization decisions are handled at the AAA server and the fact that the reasons for a decision are not communicated to the authenticator, which knows only the final result. On channel binding, the procedures are needed so that a compromised intermediate authenticator cannot give the peer and the EAP server unverified and conflicting information about the service. On transport, the architecture may need several protocols to carry keys between the parties involved, so requirements for each of those protocols, and the parameters they carry, must be developed; the use of the existing AAA protocols for carrying EAP messages and keying material must be examined, and the relation between transport identities and keying identities must be explored.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are about damage control and clarity. A key that is stolen must not unlock the keys it was derived from. Every key needs a name, a lifetime and a stated purpose. Both sides of the re-authentication must know exactly which service they are talking about, so that a rogue device in the middle cannot tell them different stories.

sections.title: Use Cases and Related Work
sections.content:
A number of EAP methods support fast re-authentication. EAP-SIM (RFC 4186) and EAP-AKA (RFC 4187) bootstrap fast re-authentication from the keys generated during the initial full authentication. In response to the usual EAP-Request/Identity, the peer sends a specially formatted identity indicating that it wants a fast re-authentication. A single round trip verifies knowledge of the existing keys and provides fresh nonces for generating new keys, followed by EAP success. In the end it takes a single local round trip between the peer and the authenticator, followed by another round trip between the peer and the EAP server. Because AKA is based on symmetric-key cryptography, its processing latency is minimal.

EAP-TTLS and PEAP support TLS session resumption for fast re-authentication: during the TLS handshake the client includes the message ID of the session it wishes to resume, and the server echoes it back if it agrees. EAP-FAST (RFC 4851) supports TLS session resumption and additionally allows the stateless session resumption of RFC 5077. For all three, there are still two round trips between the peer and the EAP server, in addition to the local round trip for the identity exchange. To improve on this, fast re-authentication needs to reduce the number of round trips overall, and optimal performance could come from eliminating the EAP-Request/Identity and EAP-Response/Identity messages and allowing a single round trip between the peer and a local re-authentication server.

In IEEE 802.11r, access points are grouped into mobility domains. Initial authentication to any AP in a mobility domain requires EAP, but handover between APs within the domain does not. Inside the domain are sets of security associations supporting key transfers between APs. In one model, a small number of devices called R0-KHs act as the authenticators, all EAP traffic traverses an R0-KH, and it derives the initial IEEE 802.11 keys and distributes cryptographically separate keys to APs in the domain as needed; for a deployment with M designated R0-KHs and N APs this needs M*N security associations, which scales reasonably for small M. Letting any AP act as an R0-KH needs a full mesh of N squared associations, which scales poorly. The designated R0-KH model is architecturally similar to the model proposed by HOKEY, but HOKEY allows handover between authenticators, so an 802.11r-enabled peer could move from one mobility domain to another without performing an EAP authentication.

CAPWAP allows the functions of an IEEE 802.11 access point to be split into two physical devices in enterprise deployments, with Wireless Termination Points implementing the physical and low-level MAC layers and a centralised Access Controller providing higher-level management and protocol execution. Client authentication is handled by the AC, which acts as the AAA authenticator. One CAPWAP feature is the ability to roam between WTPs without executing an EAP authentication: the AC caches the MSK from an initial EAP authentication and uses it to execute a separate four-way handshake with the station as it moves between WTPs, and the resulting keys are given to the WTP the station is associated with. CAPWAP is transparent to the station. It has no means to support roaming between access controllers, and the proposed work on EAP efficient re-authentication addresses exactly that inter-authenticator handover problem.
sections.plainLanguage: Several schemes already speed up the second login. Some authentication methods can reuse the first login's keys with one short exchange, and TLS can resume an earlier session. The 802.11 and CAPWAP specifications let a device move between access points without a full login, but each covers only part of the problem: 802.11r stops at the edge of a mobility domain, and CAPWAP stops at the edge of an access controller.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Scope
sections.content:
Because HOKEY is an authentication protocol, a large number of security-related issues surround its development and deployment. The document details the security properties inferred from RFC 4962 to which HOKEY must conform, covering the management of key context, scope, freshness and transport, resistance to attacks based on the domino effect, and authentication and authorization.

The scope of the protocol is re-authentication and handover between authenticators within a single administrative domain. The design goals may facilitate inter-technology handover and inter-administrative-domain handover, but those are outside the scope of the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The document sets out what a future protocol must protect and where it must stop. It covers movement between access points inside one operator's network. Movement between operators or between different technologies is left out.

viz.caption: THE SIX DESIGN GOALS FOR A HANDOVER KEYING PROTOCOL

items.title: Lower latency
items.text: Must meet the handover latency objectives of a mobile access network.

items.title: Lower-layer independence
items.text: Must work over heterogeneous technologies without requiring any particular lower layer.

items.title: EAP method independence
items.text: Must not require changes to existing EAP methods, nor impose requirements on future ones.

items.title: AAA compatibility
items.text: Must be compatible with RADIUS and Diameter and configurable to meet RFC 4962.

items.title: Compatibility
items.text: A peer without fast re-authentication must still work, and vice versa.

items.title: Cryptographic agility
items.text: Must not hard-code primitives that may later prove compromised.
